title: Satyakama and the we of the Gayatri
word: the Gayatri and the peace chants
hookLine: a boy tells a teacher the plain truth, and the Gayatri's we
carry: the gayatri prays as we, even alone
tomorrow: who is the who in dhiyo yo nah: the light, or the god?
last: BY ITS LIGHT ALL THIS SHINES.

cards: Record a voice note alone in your room, send it to the family group, and it still starts: hey, everyone. Nani says the Gayatri alone at her window, and its verb for the people is the same kind of word.
Dhimahi doesn't mean I meditate. It means we. Can a person pray alone and still say we?

teach.b: Dhimahi ends in -mahi, and -mahi marks we. We hold in mind, we meditate on; some readers write may we attain. Either way, never I.
That fits how many families receive the verse: not picked up alone, but given, teacher to student, at the sacred-thread ceremony. And the Upanishads tell a story about who gets let into that line.
In the Chandogya Upanishad, a boy named Satyakama wants to study the Vedas, and he knows a teacher will ask his family line. So he asks his mother, Jabala.
She tells him the truth: she worked as a servant when she was young, moved from house to house, and doesn't know who his father is. Just say you're Satyakama, son of Jabala.
He goes to the teacher Gautama and says exactly that, word for word. And the teacher answers: only a true brahmin could speak like this. Go and bring firewood.
I'll take you in; you have not left the truth.
That's the we in dhimahi: a long line of teachers and students, and one more voice joining it. A neighbor tradition shares something close.
In Matthew's Gospel, Jesus teaches a prayer that opens, in the King James Bible: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name.
Said alone, it still says our. One honest difference: it calls God Father and asks for daily bread and forgiveness. The Gayatri turns to Savitr's radiance and asks only that thoughts be stirred.

how: In many families the Gayatri is taught by a teacher or elder at the sacred-thread ceremony, and those who say it alone still say dhimahi, we; traditions differ on who receives it. Christians who say the Lord's Prayer alone still say our Father. Each prayer keeps its own words and its own name for God.

games.q: what does “the gayatri and the peace chants” mean?
o: a boy who told the plain truth, and a prayer that always says we
a boy turned away from school because of his birth
a prayer said only in large groups at a temple festival

games.q: one voice, a whole we — tap the pairs.
p: we meditate on, or may we attain
the boy taken in for telling the truth

s: Satyakama was turned away because he didn't know his father
the teacher took him in because he told the plain truth.
dhimahi is a we-word, even when one person says it
the Gayatri and the Lord's Prayer are the same prayer in two languages
both put one voice inside a we, but they name God differently and ask for different things.

games.q: a friend asks: if the Gayatri says we, is it wrong to say it by yourself at a window?
o: no: alone or with others, the verb is still we.
yes: a we-verb only counts with a group present.
only if you switch it to an I-form first.
games.why: dhimahi says we whoever is in the room: the one praying stands in a line of teachers and students, like Satyakama taken in by Gautama.

practice: If you say a daily prayer, say it now, slowly, and listen for its we. If you don't pray, close your eyes, let the breath settle, and bring to mind your teachers, the people who handed you whatever you know best.
Let each out-breath rest on the word we.

wordCard.voice: The Gayatri and the peace chants. Today's piece: dhimahi, we hold in mind, the people's half of the verse, always plural.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: dhimahi, we meditate on, or may we hold; the ending -mahi marks we.

carryVoice: Hold this line: dhimahi, the Gayatri prays as we, even alone, one more voice in a long line. More tomorrow.
